paragraphs: Music contains structure that extends beyond the next note. This paper examines why recurrent variational autoencoders struggle to represent that longer structure, even though variational autoencoders can learn meaningful compact representations of other kinds of data. The central problem is making the representation useful throughout a generated sequence.

The proposed MusicVAE uses a hierarchical decoder. It first produces an embedding for each subsequence, then generates the individual subsequences independently from those embeddings. This creates a level of organization between the overall latent code and the notes. The structure encourages the decoder to use the latent code, addressing posterior collapse, where that code ceases to contribute useful information.

In experiments on musical note sequences, the authors report dramatically better sampling, interpolation, and reconstruction than a flat baseline. These results concern generating music, moving between latent representations, and recovering existing sequences. Together, they support the value of organizing sequence generation into multiple levels when learning longer musical structure.
icml-2018-a-hierarchical-latent-vector-m.tldr: MusicVAE uses a hierarchical decoder to encourage useful latent representations and improve the modeling of long-term musical structure.

paragraphs: Categorical models assign probabilities to discrete outcomes, such as classes, words, or recommended items. When the outcome set becomes very large, their computational cost becomes a bottleneck because it grows linearly with the number of possibilities. This paper introduces augment and reduce, or A&R, to ease that computational burden.

A&R combines latent variable augmentation with stochastic variational inference. The augmentation introduces additional hidden variables into the modeling approach, while variational inference provides a tractable learning objective: a lower bound on the data's marginal likelihood. Training seeks to improve this bound instead of directly handling the original likelihood in its expensive form.

The method also broadens applicability beyond approaches designed specifically for softmax, extending to categorical models such as multinomial probit. Across several large-scale classification problems, the authors report a tighter likelihood bound and better predictions than existing approaches. The findings therefore concern both the quality of the approximation used during learning and its usefulness for classification.
icml-2018-augment-and-reduce-stochastic-.tldr: A&R combines latent variables and stochastic variational inference to make large categorical models more tractable while improving reported classification performance.

paragraphs: An agent can become good at learning new tasks quickly yet still forget the solution to a particular task when it moves on. If that task returns, the agent has to explore again. This paper studies that mismatch between rapid adaptation and retaining useful experience across recurring tasks.

The authors first introduce a formal way to construct environments that keep presenting new tasks while also repeating earlier ones. They then develop an architecture that combines an LSTM's working memory with a differentiable episodic memory. The combination is designed to support both learning during the current task and recalling information from earlier encounters.

The resulting episodic LSTM is explored in five meta-learning environments, covering bandits, navigation, and stochastic sequential decisions. These settings make task recurrence an explicit part of the evaluation. The paper's contribution is a framework and memory architecture for studying how agents can reuse particular experiences alongside their general ability to adapt to unfamiliar problems.
icml-2018-been-there-done-that-meta-lear.tldr: An episodic LSTM combines working memory with recall of past tasks to study meta-learning in environments where tasks recur.

paragraphs: Evaluating reinforcement learning is easier when researchers know what an optimal agent should do at every step. Many challenging environments lack that reference, making individual mistakes difficult to diagnose. This paper proposes a family of combinatorial games from work by Erdos, Selfridge, and Spencer as a controlled setting for such evaluation.

The games combine a small, simply parameterized environment with a linear closed-form solution for optimal behavior from any state. Their difficulty can also be changed through interpretable parameters. This combination matters because an environment can remain challenging for learning algorithms while providing a precise standard against which their choices can be assessed.

The authors use the games to compare reinforcement learning algorithms, examine generalization, compare with supervised learning, and analyze multiagent play. They also develop a self-play algorithm. The contribution is a diagnostic environment and a set of investigations into learning behavior; the abstract does not claim that deep reinforcement learning universally solves this game family.
icml-2018-can-deep-reinforcement-learnin.tldr: Erdos-Selfridge-Spencer games offer challenging reinforcement learning environments with known optimal behavior and interpretable difficulty controls.

paragraphs: Graph total-variation regularization uses relationships between graph vertices to constrain an optimization problem's solution. This paper extends the cut-pursuit algorithm to objectives containing a separable nondifferentiable component. That setting matters because useful objectives can contain terms for which ordinary derivatives are unavailable, requiring an algorithm designed to accommodate them.

The authors modify the algorithmic scheme and adapt its convergence proofs to the extended setting. They also consider problems where each vertex carries several values rather than a single scalar. For this multidimensional case, they present a heuristic approach, keeping its status distinct from the convergence analysis of the main algorithm.

The method is demonstrated on large inverse and learning problems described as difficult and ill-conditioned. Its observed performance suggests that it may make total-variation regularization practical for a wider range of applications. This is a qualified practical implication of the demonstrations, alongside the more formal contribution of extending the algorithm and its convergence analysis.
icml-2018-cut-pursuit-algorithm-for-regu.tldr: An extended cut-pursuit algorithm handles graph total-variation objectives with separable nondifferentiable terms and shows promising large-scale performance.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks learn filters from data, and those filters account for many model parameters. DCFNet changes how filters are represented: each is expressed as a limited combination of fixed basis elements. The network learns the coefficients of that combination, rather than learning every filter entry independently.

Keeping only a truncated basis expansion reduces both trainable parameters and computation. It also restricts the forms filters can take, imposing regularity through their representation. The authors test different bases and consistently observe preserved image-classification accuracy with substantially fewer parameters, particularly with Fourier-Bessel bases, but also with random bases.

The paper additionally analyzes how the network's representations respond to changes in the input. It proves stability under generic assumptions on the learned expansion coefficients, and describes that analysis as consistent with the empirical observations. The combined contribution is a more compact filter representation with experimental accuracy preservation and a conditional theoretical account of representation stability.
icml-2018-dcfnet-deep-neural-network-wit.tldr: DCFNet learns coefficients over fixed filter bases, reducing parameters and computation while maintaining accuracy in the reported image-classification experiments.

paragraphs: A neural network used for anomaly detection may first be trained for a different purpose, such as generating or compressing data. Its outputs are then adapted to identify unusual examples. This paper asks whether the network can instead be trained directly with an objective designed for anomaly detection.

The proposed method, Deep Support Vector Data Description, takes that direct approach. Moving the method into a deep-learning setting requires the network and its training procedure to satisfy particular properties. The authors demonstrate these requirements theoretically, making the design of the network and the way it is trained part of the contribution.

Experiments show the method's effectiveness on MNIST and CIFAR-10, as well as in detecting adversarial examples of stop signs from GTSRB. These demonstrations connect the anomaly-focused objective to both image benchmarks and manipulated inputs. The findings support training specifically for anomaly detection in these settings, with the theoretical work explaining why the deep adaptation requires care.
icml-2018-deep-one-class-classification-.tldr: Deep Support Vector Data Description trains a neural network directly for anomaly detection and demonstrates effectiveness on image and adversarial-example tasks.

paragraphs: Learning from multiple data sources becomes harder when some sources are adversarial. This paper studies binary classification with n sources, assuming that at most an eta fraction are adversarial. The question is how much additional data collaborative learning requires compared with learning the same hypothesis class from one distribution.

The authors measure that extra burden through sample-complexity overhead: the ratio of the sample requirements in the two settings. They present an algorithm with overhead O(eta n + ln n) and prove that this dependence is optimal in the worst case. The bound separates a term tied to adversarial sources from a logarithmic term tied to the total source count.

This result characterizes the worst-case sample cost of collaboration under the stated corruption assumption. It does not settle computational efficiency: the paper separately discusses challenges in obtaining a computationally efficient algorithm with small overhead. The distinction matters because an optimal data requirement and an efficient implementation are different achievements.
icml-2018-do-outliers-ruin-collaboration.tldr: The paper establishes a worst-case optimal sample overhead of O(eta n + ln n) for binary learning across partly adversarial sources.

paragraphs: Information-theoretic Bayesian optimization uses information about an objective to guide the search for its global optimum. Such approaches can perform well, but choosing where to evaluate next can itself require substantial computation. The paper targets this overhead, along with implementation approximations and restrictions on the kernels used to model the objective.

The proposed method, FITBO, avoids sampling the global minimizer. Removing that step substantially reduces computational overhead, while working in the output space gives the method fewer restrictions on kernel choice than existing approaches. The contribution concerns making information-based search more practical without giving up its reported optimization strengths.

Empirical results indicate that FITBO retains the performance associated with information-theoretic Bayesian optimization and runs faster even than simpler approaches such as Expected Improvement. This finding links search performance with the cost of making search decisions. It is an experimental result about the evaluated method, rather than a guarantee that FITBO is fastest on every optimization problem.
icml-2018-fast-information-theoretic-bay.tldr: FITBO avoids sampling the global minimizer to reduce information-theoretic Bayesian optimization overhead while retaining strong empirical search performance.

paragraphs: Neural networks trained by backpropagation can struggle with classes seen only a few times. This becomes especially consequential when rare labels are common, as in language modeling. One possible response is an external memory that stores recent activations and labels so the model can quickly reuse those observations.

This paper explores a simpler alternative: treating part of the network's existing parameters as fast memory stores. The approach can retain information over longer intervals than a traditional memory without requiring additional space or computation. Its central idea is to make rapid memorization part of the parametric model itself.

On an Omniglot image curriculum task, the method binds novel classes faster. It also improves word-based language modeling on GigaWord news, Project Gutenberg books, and WikiText-103 articles. The reported WikiText-103 perplexity is 29.2, described as state of the art. These results show benefits across both newly encountered image classes and language tasks containing infrequently observed labels.
icml-2018-fast-parametric-learning-with-.tldr: Using existing model parameters as fast memory improves learning from rare observations without additional space or computation.

paragraphs: Predicting what happens next in video or audio requires understanding how meaningful events fit together over time. The relevant structure can extend beyond the immediate past and can combine smaller events into larger activities. Context-free grammars can express such structure, but conventional grammar parsers expect sequences that already contain discrete symbols.

The paper generalizes the Earley parser to sequences that have neither segment boundaries nor labels. It combines a grammar parser with a classifier to find the optimal segmentation and labeling. This connects the classifier's interpretation of the data with grammatical constraints on how the resulting events can fit together.

The integrated system also makes top-down predictions about future events using the grammar. Experiments on future human activity prediction show significant improvements over other approaches. The result supports combining recognition with structured sequence reasoning: the method uses an account of the larger activity both to interpret the observed sequence and to anticipate what may follow.
icml-2018-generalized-earley-parser-brid.tldr: A generalized Earley parser combines classification and grammar-based reasoning to segment unlabeled sequences and predict future human activities.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can be slowed by workers that finish their computations late. Gradient coding addresses these stragglers by organizing computations so learning can proceed despite missing worker results. This paper develops new exact gradient codes using cyclic MDS codes, reporting favorable parameter coverage and algorithmic complexity compared with existing solutions.

The authors also introduce an approximate version of gradient coding, allowing the computed gradient to differ from the exact one. Their main construction uses the normalized adjacency matrix of an expander graph. This approach can substantially reduce worker computation compared with exact gradient coding, making approximation an explicit option in the design.

Experiments on Amazon EC2 find that approximate gradient coding produces generalization error very close to that obtained with the full gradient while requiring significantly less worker computation. The result connects an approximation in distributed computation to the quality of the learned model. It supports the practical value of approximate codes in the tested setting alongside the new exact constructions.
icml-2018-gradient-coding-from-cyclic-md.tldr: New exact and approximate gradient codes mitigate distributed-learning stragglers, with approximate codes reducing computation while preserving similar reported generalization error.

paragraphs: Increasing network depth is a major route to stronger image recognition, usually accomplished by stacking more convolutional layers or blocks. This paper introduces another way to deepen computation: placing an order on the channels inside an existing layer or block and computing their outputs gradually.

The ordering adds structure within the computation already present in the network. According to the authors, it increases depth and learning capacity without adding computational cost. They also report that the ordering removes overlap singularities, connecting this architectural change with faster convergence and better performance. The proposed benefit therefore involves both representational capacity and training behavior.

Networks built with this gradual channel-wise computation achieve reported state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR and ImageNet. These experiments support computation order as an architectural design choice for large-scale recognition. The key contribution is showing that increased depth can come from reorganizing how channels are computed, broadening the usual strategy of adding successive layers or blocks.
icml-2018-gradually-updated-neural-netwo.tldr: Ordering channel computations increases network depth and capacity without additional computation, with reported state-of-the-art image-recognition results.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because useful feedback arrives infrequently. An agent trying to learn a complex behavior from scratch may therefore struggle to explore productively. Scheduled Auxiliary Control, or SAC-X, addresses this setting by giving the agent a collection of general auxiliary tasks to learn alongside one another.

The agent learns these tasks through off-policy reinforcement learning. A central part of the approach is learning how to schedule and execute the auxiliary policies. Their role extends beyond providing additional learning objectives: actively selecting among them helps the agent explore its environment in ways that support learning under sparse rewards.

The authors demonstrate SAC-X in several challenging robotic manipulation settings, reporting that it enables complex behavior to be learned from scratch with multiple sparse reward signals. The contribution links task learning and exploration through a learned schedule. Its experimental findings support auxiliary policies as useful tools for reaching informative experience when rewards alone provide little immediate guidance.
icml-2018-learning-by-playing-solving-sp.tldr: SAC-X learns to schedule auxiliary policies that improve exploration and support learning complex robotic behaviors from sparse rewards.

paragraphs: Training large implicit generative models with the method of moments requires many useful statistical properties to match. Choosing those properties manually is difficult, especially when millions are needed. This paper introduces the Method of Learned Moments, or MoLM, to construct and improve the moments through a separate neural network.

The moment network supplies moments from its hidden units and from gradients of its output with respect to its parameters. To guide their learning, the authors use asymptotic theory: useful moments should reduce the asymptotic variance of estimated model parameters. This turns moment selection into a learned objective with a statistical motivation.

On CIFAR-10, MoLM-trained generators achieve significantly better Inception Scores and Frechet Inception Distances than generators trained with the specified gradient-penalty and spectral-normalization adversarial objectives. The authors also report nearly perfect Multi-Scale Structural Similarity Scores on CelebA and high-quality 128-by-128 samples. These findings support learned moments as an effective training approach for the evaluated neural image generators.
icml-2018-learning-implicit-generative-m.tldr: MoLM learns statistically motivated moments for training implicit image generators and reports improvements over specified adversarial training objectives.

paragraphs: A function can be learnable from data and efficiently optimizable, yet optimizing its learned approximation can still produce a very poor answer for the true function. This paper examines that problem for combinatorial optimization, motivated by negative results for submodular functions. The gap concerns using learned predictions to choose a good solution.

The authors investigate the source of this difficulty and propose an alternative criterion for optimization from sampled data. Under that criterion, they prove a tight equivalence: a function class is optimizable if and only if it is learnable. The criterion is central to interpreting the result; the equivalence does not erase the earlier failures of surrogate optimization.

The paper also supplies efficient, scalable optimization algorithms for several function classes and demonstrates their utility in selecting trending social media items. The work therefore combines a theoretical reframing with algorithms and an application. Its main message is that the definition of successful optimization from data determines how learning guarantees can support decision-making.
icml-2018-learning-to-optimize-combinato.tldr: An alternative criterion for combinatorial optimization from samples yields a tight equivalence between learnability and optimizability.

paragraphs: Training examples can mislead a neural network when labels are corrupted or the training set is biased. Assigning different weights to examples can help, but existing approaches often need carefully tuned schedules or regularization settings. This paper learns the weights through a meta-learning procedure guided by clean validation data.

The method considers the direction in which each example's gradient would move the model. For the current mini-batch, it initializes example weights at zero and takes a meta gradient step to reduce loss on a clean, unbiased validation set. This connects an example's influence during training to whether that influence helps the validation objective.

The authors report strong results on class imbalance and corrupted-label problems even with little clean validation data. They describe the approach as applicable to any deep network without additional hyperparameter tuning. Its practical appeal is automatically adjusting training influence, while the clean and unbiased validation set supplies the reference needed to judge which updates are useful.
icml-2018-learning-to-reweight-examples-.tldr: A meta-learning method weights training examples by how their gradient directions help a small, clean, unbiased validation set.

paragraphs: Predicting another agent's behavior can require reasoning about its desires, beliefs, and intentions. This paper develops a Theory of Mind neural network, or ToMnet, that learns models of other agents through meta-learning. The aim is to use experience across agents to interpret a newly encountered agent from limited observations.

ToMnet learns a prior model of how agents behave. A small number of behavioral observations then supports richer predictions about a particular agent's characteristics and mental states. This combines general expectations learned across a population with evidence from the individual being observed, providing a basis for anticipating its future behavior.

The authors test the system in simple gridworlds with random, algorithmic, and deep reinforcement learning agents. ToMnet learns to model these varied populations and passes classic theory-of-mind tasks, including the Sally-Anne test for recognizing false beliefs. These results demonstrate the reported capacities in controlled agent environments, where another agent's belief can differ from the actual world.
icml-2018-machine-theory-of-mind-2640780.tldr: ToMnet meta-learns models of other agents and uses limited observations to predict behavior and recognize false beliefs in gridworld tasks.

paragraphs: In multiagent reinforcement learning, another player's goals may be hidden even though those goals affect rewards. An agent must therefore use observed behavior to infer what the other player wants. This paper studies that imperfect-information setting, where successful decisions depend on the hidden goals of both interacting agents.

The proposed Self Other-Modeling method uses an agent's own policy to predict the other agent's actions. It updates a belief about the other's hidden goal as interaction unfolds. The policy thus serves two purposes: guiding the agent's behavior and helping it interpret another player's behavior in terms of possible goals.

The authors evaluate the approach on three tasks spanning cooperation and competition. They find that agents learn better policies when they use their estimates of other players' goals. These results support online goal inference as a useful component of decision-making in the tested settings, and show how an agent's own policy can contribute to that inference.
icml-2018-modeling-others-using-oneself-.tldr: Self Other-Modeling uses an agent's own policy to infer another player's hidden goal and improve decisions in cooperative and competitive tasks.

paragraphs: Optimization over a complicated feasible set can make projection prohibitively expensive. Conditional gradient methods provide a projection-free approach. This paper extends conditional gradient sliding to non-convex problems, building on a method that combines accelerated gradients with Frank-Wolfe and reduces gradient computations in convex optimization.

The authors propose non-convex conditional gradient sliding methods and analyze their convergence in batch, stochastic, and finite-sum settings. They also introduce a variance-reduced version, NCGS-VR. For finite-sum problems, this version has a faster convergence rate than batch NCGS, showing how variance reduction can strengthen the approach in that setting.

Across all three settings, the paper reports theoretical and practical advantages over corresponding Frank-Wolfe methods. The contribution is therefore both an algorithmic extension and an analysis of its behavior beyond convex optimization. Its relevance is strongest for the stated computational obstacle: problems where respecting constraints through projection is too costly and a projection-free method offers a useful route forward.
icml-2018-non-convex-conditional-gradien.tldr: Non-convex conditional gradient sliding improves on Frank-Wolfe counterparts across three optimization settings while avoiding expensive projections.

paragraphs: Some statistical problems contain an expectation inside another expectation. Estimating them requires an outer Monte Carlo calculation whose terms depend on additional estimated quantities. This paper investigates what happens statistically when these estimators are nested, including cases with several levels of nesting.

The authors establish conditions for convergence and derive convergence rates, then provide empirical evidence matching those rates. They also identify pitfalls of naive nesting and give guidance for avoiding them. For certain classes of problems, they develop reformulations that replace nested expectations with a single expectation and improve convergence rates.

The results are applied to a new estimator for discrete Bayesian experimental design and to error bounds for a class of variational objectives. These applications show why the nesting analysis matters beyond a mathematical detail: it affects how estimators should be constructed and what accuracy can be expected. The improved single-expectation formulations apply to the identified classes, rather than to every nested problem.
icml-2018-on-nesting-monte-carlo-estimat.tldr: The paper establishes convergence conditions and rates for nested Monte Carlo estimation and improves certain problems through single-expectation reformulations.

paragraphs: A team of agents may have access to global information during training while each agent must act using only local observations after training. QMIX addresses how to exploit that richer training information while obtaining coordinated policies that can run in a decentralized way.

The method estimates a joint action-value by combining individual agents' values through a nonlinear network. Each individual value depends only on local observations. QMIX constrains the combination to be monotonic in those values. This structure makes joint-value maximization tractable during off-policy learning and guarantees consistency between the centralized and decentralized policies.

The authors evaluate QMIX on challenging StarCraft II micromanagement tasks and report significant improvements over existing value-based multiagent methods. The findings support the combination of expressive nonlinear mixing with a structural constraint that keeps decentralized choices consistent with the central value estimate. The guarantee concerns that consistency; the reported performance advantage comes from the evaluated tasks.
icml-2018-qmix-monotonic-value-function-.tldr: QMIX mixes local agent values monotonically to support centralized training and consistent decentralized decisions, improving reported StarCraft II performance.

paragraphs: Online hypothesis testing requires choosing a rejection threshold before seeing the current test's p-value. The decision can depend on past tests, but not on present or future results. The goal is to control the false discovery rate up to every time point, even when the sequence of tests may continue indefinitely.

SAFFRON manages an error budget, called alpha-wealth, allocating it across tests and earning some back when it makes discoveries. Its adaptive component estimates how much of the allocated budget goes to true null hypotheses. That estimate informs the thresholds, distinguishing it from earlier non-adaptive budget-allocation methods.

The authors frame SAFFRON as an online counterpart to the adaptive Storey-BH procedure used offline. They demonstrate greater power than non-adaptive counterparts such as LORD, meaning improved ability to make discoveries within the false-discovery-control framework. The contribution combines sequential budget management with an estimate of where the budget is spent, while respecting the requirement that each threshold use only past information.
icml-2018-saffron-an-adaptive-algorithm-.tldr: SAFFRON adaptively allocates an online testing error budget and demonstrates greater discovery power than non-adaptive counterparts.

paragraphs: A tighter evidence lower bound may appear to be an automatically better training objective for a latent-variable model. This paper challenges that assumption when training a generative model and an inference network together. It shows theoretically and empirically that tightening the bound can weaken the inference network's learning signal.

The mechanism is a reduction in the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient estimator. A bound can more closely approximate its target while providing less useful gradients for learning the inference network. This separates the quality of an objective as an approximation from its effectiveness as a tool for training both networks.

The authors introduce PIWAE, MIWAE, and CIWAE, each containing standard IWAE as a special case. All three can improve over IWAE, including when assessed using IWAE's own target. The results further suggest that PIWAE may improve training of both the inference and generative networks simultaneously. That simultaneous benefit remains a suggested possibility in the stated findings.
icml-2018-tighter-variational-bounds-are.tldr: Tighter variational bounds can weaken inference-network gradients, motivating three alternatives that can outperform IWAE.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks can require too much memory for deployment on many devices. Compression commonly simplifies weights through pruning or quantization. Weightless adds an encoding scheme designed together with such simplification techniques, addressing how the simplified weights themselves are stored.

The encoding uses a Bloomier filter, a probabilistic data structure that saves space by permitting random errors. The method relies on neural networks tolerating these imperfections and retrains the network around the introduced errors. This makes the encoding and subsequent learning connected parts of the compression approach, rather than treating storage errors independently of model behavior.

The authors report weight compression of up to 496 times without a loss of model accuracy, with up to a 1.51-fold improvement over the stated state of the art. These are maximum reported gains, rather than uniform compression guarantees. The findings show that a lossy storage representation can work effectively with weight simplification and retraining while preserving accuracy in the reported results.
icml-2018-weightless-lossy-weight-encodi.tldr: Weightless combines probabilistic weight encoding with retraining, achieving reported compression of up to 496 times without accuracy loss.
